The Schmidt number and partially entanglement breaking channels in infinite dimensions

This work is partially supported by the program ”Mathematical control theory” of Russian Academy of Sciences, by the federal target program ”Scientific and pedagogical staff of innovative Russia” (program 1.2.1, contract P 938), by the analytical departmental target program ”Development of scientific potential of the higher school” (project 2.1.1/500) and by RFBR grants 09-01-00424-a and 10-01-00139-a.
M.E. Shirokov Affiliation: Steklov Mathematical Institute, RAS, Moscow Email: msh@mi.ras.ru
Abstract

A definition of the Schmidt number of a state of an infinite dimensional bipartite quantum system is given and properties of the corresponding family of Schmidt classes are considered. The existence of states with a given Schmidt number such that any their countable convex decomposition does not contain pure states with finite Schmidt rank is established.

Partially entanglement breaking channels in infinite dimensions are studied. Several properties of these channels well known in finite dimensions are generalized to the infinite dimensional case. At the same time, the existence of partially entanglement breaking channels (in particular, entanglement breaking channels) such that all operators in any their Kraus representations have infinite rank is proved.

1 Introduction

The Schmidt rank of a pure state and its extension to mixed states called the Schmidt number are important quantitative characteristics of entanglement in bipartite quantum systems.

The Schmidt rank of a pure state of bipartite system A​BAB determined by a unit vector |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle is defined as the number of nonzero terms in the Schmidt decomposition

|ψ⟩=∑iλi​|αi⟩⊗|βi⟩|\psi\rangle=\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}|\alpha_{i}\rangle\otimes|\beta_{i}\rangle

of this vector, it coincides with the rank of the reduced states.

The Schmidt number of a mixed state ω\omega of a finite dimensional bipartite system A​BAB is defined in [18] as the minimum over all its decompositions into convex combination of pure states of the maximal Schmidt rank of these pure states (see Section 3). In [18] it is shown that the Schmidt number does not increase under LOCC-operations and that the set of states with the Schmidt number not exceeding kk (the Schmidt class of order kk) can be characterized in terms of kk-positive maps. In the subsequent papers [12, 16, 17] different properties of the Schmidt number and of the family of the Schmidt classes are considered. In particular, the notion of kk-Schmidt witnesses generalizing the notion of entanglement witnesses is introduced and analyzed.

By using the Schmidt number the notion of partially entanglement breaking quantum channels is introduced in [3]. It turns out that this notion is closely related to the necessary condition of nondecreasing of the Holevo quantity of an ensemble of quantum states under action of a quantum channel [14, Theorem 1].

This paper is devoted to infinite-dimensional generalizations of the above concepts. It is partially motivated by author’s intension to extend the above-mentioned result in [14] to ”continuous variable” systems and channels.

In Section 3 a natural generalization of the Schmidt number to states of infinite dimensional bipartite quantum systems is considered. Since existence of non-countably decomposable separable states (see [5]) makes the finite dimensional formula for the Schmidt number non-adequate, the ”continuous” modification of this formula (based on the notion of the essential supremum of a function with respect to a given measure) is proposed. It is shown that this formula gives a reasonable definition of the Schmidt number in the sense that the corresponding Schmidt classes (the sets of states with the Schmidt number ≤k\leq k) coincide with the convex closures of the sets of pure states with the Schmidt rank ≤k\leq k.

Properties of the Schmidt classes in infinite dimensions are considered in Section 4. In particular, the characterization the Schmidt class of order kk in terms of kk-positive maps (generalizing Theorem 1 in [18]) is given. It is shown that an arbitrary state in the Schmidt class of order kk can be represented as a barycenter of a probability measure supported by pure states with the Schmidt rank ≤k\leq k. At the same time, the existence of states with a given Schmidt number such that any their countable convex decomposition does not contain pure states with a finite Schmidt rank is established.

A definition and some properties of partially entanglement breaking channels in infinite dimensions are considered in Section 5. In contrast to the finite dimensional case, the class of kk-partially entanglement breaking channels does not coincide with the class of channels having the Kraus representation consisting of operators of rank ≤k\leq k (the latter is a proper subclass of the former). Moreover, the existence of partially entanglement breaking channels (in particular, of entanglement breaking channels) such that all operators in any their Kraus representations have infinite rank is proved.

2 Basic notations

We will use the following notations:

ℋ,ℋ′,𝒦\mathcal{H},\mathcal{H}^{\prime},\mathcal{K}

– separable Hilbert spaces;

𝔅⁡(ℋ)\mathfrak{B}(\mathcal{H})

– the Banach space of all bounded operators in ℋ\mathcal{H};

𝔗⁡(ℋ)\mathfrak{T}(\mathcal{H})

– the Banach space of all trace-class operators in ℋ\mathcal{H};

𝔗+​(ℋ)\mathfrak{T}_{+}(\mathcal{H})

– the cone of all positive trace-class operators in ℋ\mathcal{H};

𝔖⁡(ℋ)\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H})

– the subset of 𝔗+​(ℋ)\mathfrak{T}_{+}(\mathcal{H}) consisting of operators with a unit trace.

The unit operator in a Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H} and the identity transformation of the space 𝔗⁡(ℋ)\mathfrak{T}(\mathcal{H}) are denoted IℋI_{\mathcal{H}} and Idℋ\mathrm{Id}_{\mathcal{H}} correspondingly.

Operators in 𝔖⁡(ℋ)\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}) are denoted ρ,σ,ω,…\rho,\sigma,\omega,... and called density operators or states since each density operator uniquely defines a normal state on 𝔅⁡(ℋ)\mathfrak{B}(\mathcal{H}).

We denote by cl⁡(𝒜)\mathrm{cl}(\mathcal{A}), co⁡(𝒜)\mathrm{co}(\mathcal{A}), co¯​(𝒜)\overline{\mathrm{co}}(\mathcal{A}) and extr⁡(𝒜)\mathrm{extr}(\mathcal{A}) the closure, the convex hull, the convex closure and the set of all extreme points of a subset 𝒜\mathcal{A} of a linear topological space correspondingly [9, 1, 11].

The set of all Borel probability measures on a closed subset 𝒜⊆𝔖⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}) endowed with the topology of weak convergence is denoted 𝒫⁡(𝒜)\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{A}) [2, 10]. This set can be considered as a complete separable metric space [10]. The barycenter b​(μ)\textbf{b}(\mu) of a measure μ\mu in 𝒫⁡(𝒜)\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{A}) is the state in co¯​(𝒜)\overline{\mathrm{co}}(\mathcal{A}) defined by the Bochner integral

b​(μ)=∫𝒜ρ​μ​(𝑑ρ).\textbf{b}(\mu)=\int_{\mathcal{A}}\rho\mu(d\rho).

For an arbitrary subset ℬ⊆co¯​(𝒜)\,\mathcal{B}\subseteq\overline{\mathrm{co}}(\mathcal{A})\, let 𝒫ℬ​(𝒜)\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{B}}(\mathcal{A}) be the subset of 𝒫⁡(𝒜)\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{A}) consisting of all measures with the barycenter in ℬ\mathcal{B}.

A finite or infinite collection of states {ρi}⊂𝒜⊆𝔖⁡(ℋ)\{\rho_{i}\}\subset\mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}) with the corresponding probability distribution {πi}\{\pi_{i}\} is conventionally called ensemble and denoted {πi,ρi}\{\pi_{i},\rho_{i}\}. An ensemble can be considered as an atomic (discrete) measure in 𝒫⁡(𝒜)\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{A}). The barycenter of this measure is the average state ∑iπi​ρi\sum_{i}\pi_{i}\rho_{i} of the corresponding ensemble.

A positive trace-preserving linear map Φ:𝔗⁡(ℋ)→𝔗⁡(ℋ′)\Phi:\mathfrak{T}(\mathcal{H})\rightarrow\mathfrak{T}(\mathcal{H}^{\prime}) such that the dual map Φ∗:𝔅⁡(ℋ′)→𝔅⁡(ℋ)\Phi^{*}:\mathfrak{B}(\mathcal{H}^{\prime})\rightarrow\mathfrak{B}(\mathcal{H}) is completely positive is called quantum channel [4, 8]. The set of all quantum channels from 𝔗⁡(ℋ)\mathfrak{T}(\mathcal{H}) to 𝔗⁡(ℋ′)\mathfrak{T}(\mathcal{H}^{\prime}) is denoted 𝔉⁡(ℋ,ℋ′)\mathfrak{F}(\mathcal{H},\mathcal{H}^{\prime}).

3 The Schmidt number

Let ℋ\mathcal{H} and 𝒦\mathcal{K} be separable Hilbert spaces. The Schmidt rank SR⁡(ω)\mathrm{SR}(\omega) of a pure state ω\omega in 𝔖⁡(ℋ⊗𝒦)\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{K}) can be defined as the rank of the isomorphic states Tr𝒦​ω\mathrm{Tr}_{\mathcal{K}}\omega and Trℋ​ω\mathrm{Tr}_{\mathcal{H}}\omega.

If the spaces ℋ\mathcal{H} and 𝒦\mathcal{K} are finite dimensional then the Schmidt number of an arbitrary state ω\omega in 𝔖⁡(ℋ⊗𝒦)\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{K}) is defined in [18] as follows

SN⁡(ω)=inf∑iπi​ωi=ωsupiSR⁡(ωi)\mathrm{SN}(\omega)=\inf_{\sum_{i}\pi_{i}\omega_{i}=\omega}\sup_{i}\mathrm{SR}(\omega_{i}) (1)

(the infimum is over all ensembles {πi,ωi}\{\pi_{i},\omega_{i}\} of pure states with the average state ω\omega). By using the Caratheodory theorem it is easy to show that for each natural kk the set 𝔖k​(ℋ⊗𝒦)={ω∈𝔖⁡(ℋ⊗𝒦)|SN⁡(ω)≤k}\mathfrak{S}_{k}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{K})=\{\omega\in\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{K})\,|\,\mathrm{SN}(\omega)\leq k\} is compact and coincides with the convex hull of all pure states having the Schmidt rank ≤k\leq k. This implies that the function ω↦SN⁡(ω)\omega\mapsto\mathrm{SN}(\omega) is lower semicontinuous on the set 𝔖⁡(ℋ⊗𝒦)\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{K}). Thus we have the increasing finite sequence11 1 Here and in what follows we will often write 𝔖k\mathfrak{S}_{k} instead of 𝔖k​(ℋ⊗𝒦)\mathfrak{S}_{k}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{K}) for brevity.

𝔖1⊂𝔖2⊂𝔖3⊂…⊂𝔖n−1⊂𝔖n=𝔖⁡(ℋ⊗𝒦)\mathfrak{S}_{1}\subset\mathfrak{S}_{2}\subset\mathfrak{S}_{3}\subset...\subset\mathfrak{S}_{n-1}\subset\mathfrak{S}_{n}=\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{K})

of compact sets, where 𝔖1\mathfrak{S}_{1} is the set of separable (non-entangled) states and n=min⁡{dimℋ,dim𝒦}n=\min\{\dim\mathcal{H},\dim\mathcal{K}\}.

If the spaces ℋ\mathcal{H} and 𝒦\mathcal{K} are infinite dimensional then the right side of (1) is well defined but can not be used as an adequate definition of the Schmidt number. This follows from existence of separable states in 𝔖⁡(ℋ⊗𝒦)\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{K}) (called non-countably decomposable), which can not be decomposed into a countable convex combination of product pure states [5]. The nonexistence of a decomposition into product pure states shows that the right side of (1) is >1>1 for any such separable state ω\omega contradicting to the natural requirement for the Schmidt number.22 2 This problem is similar to the problem arising in infinite dimensional generalization of the convex roof construction of entanglement monotones: the existence of non-countably decomposable separable states makes the discrete version of this construction not adequate (see Remark 9 in [13]).

We will show below that a reasonable generalization of definition (1) to the infinite dimensional case is given by the following formula

SN⁡(ω)=infμ∈𝒫{ω}​(extr​𝔖​(ℋ⊗𝒦))ess​supμ​SR​(⋅)\mathrm{SN}(\omega)=\inf_{\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{\{\omega\}}(\mathrm{extr}\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{K}))}\mathrm{ess}\,\mathrm{sup}_{\mu}\mathrm{SR}(\cdot) (2)

where "​ess​supμ​""\mathrm{ess}\,\mathrm{sup}_{\mu}" means the essential supremum with respect to the measure μ\mu [1, Section 13.1]. Note that ess​supμ​SR​(⋅)=‖SR‖∞\mathrm{ess}\,\mathrm{sup}_{\mu}\mathrm{SR}(\cdot)=\|\mathrm{SR}\|_{\infty} – the norm of the function SR\mathrm{SR} in the space L∞​(X,μ)L^{\infty}(X,\mu), where X=extr​𝔖​(ℋ⊗𝒦)X=\mathrm{extr}\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{K}).

Proposition 1. A) The function SN⁡(ω)\,\mathrm{SN}(\omega) defined by (2) is lower semicontinuous on 𝔖⁡(ℋ⊗𝒦)\,\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{K}). For each state ω∈𝔖⁡(ℋ⊗𝒦)\,\omega\in\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{K}) the infimum in (2) is achieved at some measure in extr​𝒫{ω}​(extr​𝔖​(ℋ⊗𝒦))\,\mathrm{extr}\mathcal{P}_{\{\omega\}}(\mathrm{extr}\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{K})).

B) For each natural kk the set 𝔖k​(ℋ⊗𝒦)={ω∈𝔖⁡(ℋ⊗𝒦)|SN⁡(ω)≤k}\,\mathfrak{S}_{k}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{K})=\{\omega\in\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{K})\,|\,\mathrm{SN}(\omega)\leq k\}, where SN⁡(ω)\mathrm{SN}(\omega) is defined by (2), is closed and convex. It coincides with the convex closure of all pure states in 𝔖⁡(ℋ⊗𝒦)\,\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{K}) having the Schmidt rank ≤k\leq k.

C) If ω\,\omega is a finite rank state in 𝔖⁡(ℋ⊗𝒦)\,\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{K}) then the value SN⁡(ω)\,\mathrm{SN}(\omega) defined by (2) coincides with the value SN⁡(ω)\,\mathrm{SN}(\omega) defined by (1).

Proof. Since the nonnegative function ω↦SR⁡(ω)\omega\mapsto\mathrm{SR}(\omega) is lower semicontinuous on extr​𝔖​(ℋ⊗𝒦)\mathrm{extr}\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{K}), the first assertion of the proposition follows from Proposition 6.1 in the Appendix.

The second assertion follows from the first one and Lemma 1 in [5].

To prove the third assertion assume that the right side of (2) is equal to k<+∞k<+\infty. Equality of the right side of (1) to kk follows from coincidence of the convex hull and the convex closure of the closed subset

𝔖kω={ϖ∈extr​𝔖​(supp​ω)|SR⁡(ϖ)≤k}\mathfrak{S}^{\omega}_{k}=\{\varpi\in\mathrm{extr}\mathfrak{S}(\mathrm{supp}\omega)\,|\,\mathrm{SR}(\varpi)\leq k\}

of the finite-dimensional space 𝔗⁡(supp​ω)\mathfrak{T}(\mathrm{supp}\omega) (see [1, Corollary 5.33]). □\square

The following proposition generalizes Proposition 1 in [18] to the infinite dimensional case.

Proposition 2. The Schmidt number of a state of an infinite-dimensional bipartite system (defined by (2)) does not increase under LOCC-operations.

This proposition can be reduced to Proposition 1 in [18] by using the following approximation result.

Lemma 1. Let {Pn}\{P_{n}\} and {Qn}\{Q_{n}\} be increasing sequences of finite rank projectors strongly converging respectively to IℋI_{\mathcal{H}} and to I𝒦I_{\mathcal{K}}. For an arbitrary state ω∈𝔖⁡(ℋ⊗𝒦)\omega\in\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{K}) let ωn=(Tr​Pn⊗Qn⋅ω)−1​Pn⊗Qn⋅ω⋅Pn⊗Qn\,\omega_{n}=(\mathrm{Tr}P_{n}\otimes Q_{n}\cdot\omega)^{-1}P_{n}\otimes Q_{n}\cdot\omega\cdot P_{n}\otimes Q_{n}. Then

limn→+∞SN⁡(ωn)=SN⁡(ω).\lim_{n\rightarrow+\infty}\mathrm{SN}(\omega_{n})=\mathrm{SN}(\omega).

If SN⁡(ω)<+∞\,\mathrm{SN}(\omega)<+\infty then there exists n0n_{0} such that SN⁡(ωn)=SN⁡(ω)\,\mathrm{SN}(\omega_{n})=\mathrm{SN}(\omega) for all n≥n0n\geq n_{0}.

Proof. By lower semicontinuity of the Schmidt number (Proposition 3A) it suffices to show that

SN⁡(ωn)≤SN⁡(ω),∀n.\mathrm{SN}(\omega_{n})\leq\mathrm{SN}(\omega),\quad\forall n. (3)

Since the state ω\omega belongs to the convex closure of the set 𝔖SN⁡(ω)p\mathfrak{S}^{p}_{\mathrm{SN}(\omega)} of pure states with the Schmidt rank ≤SN⁡(ω)\leq\mathrm{SN}(\omega) (Proposition 3B), there exists a sequence {ωm}\{\omega_{m}\} from the convex hull of the set 𝔖SN⁡(ω)p\mathfrak{S}^{p}_{\mathrm{SN}(\omega)} converging to the state ω\omega such that limn→+∞SN⁡(ωm)=SN⁡(ω)\lim_{n\rightarrow+\infty}\mathrm{SN}(\omega_{m})=\mathrm{SN}(\omega). For each mm inequality (3) with ω=ωm\omega=\omega_{m} is directly verified. By lower semicontinuity of the Schmidt number passing to the limit as m→+∞m\rightarrow+\infty implies (3). □\square

4 Some properties of the Schmidt classes 𝔖k\mathfrak{S}_{k}

If dimℋ=dim𝒦=+∞\,\dim\mathcal{H}=\dim\mathcal{K}=+\infty we have the increasing infinite sequence

𝔖1⊂𝔖2⊂𝔖3⊂…⊂𝔖n−1⊂𝔖n⊂…\mathfrak{S}_{1}\subset\mathfrak{S}_{2}\subset\mathfrak{S}_{3}\subset...\subset\mathfrak{S}_{n-1}\subset\mathfrak{S}_{n}\subset...

of closed convex subsets of 𝔖⁡(ℋ⊗𝒦)\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{K}), where 𝔖1\mathfrak{S}_{1} is the set of separable (nonentangled) states.

Let 𝔖kp\mathfrak{S}^{p}_{k} be the closed subset of 𝔖k\mathfrak{S}_{k} consisting of pure states.

Proposition 3. A) An arbitrary state in 𝔖k\mathfrak{S}_{k} can be represented as a barycenter of some measure in extr​𝒫​(𝔖kp)\,\mathrm{extr}\mathcal{P}(\mathfrak{S}^{p}_{k}).

B) There exist states ω\omega in 𝔖k∖𝔖k−1\;\mathfrak{S}_{k}\setminus\mathfrak{S}_{k-1}\, such that the operator ω−λ​σ\,\omega-\lambda\sigma is not positive for any λ>0\lambda>0 and any pure state σ\sigma with a finite Schmidt rank.33 3 It is assumed that 𝔖0=∅\mathfrak{S}_{0}=\emptyset, so that 𝔖1∖𝔖0=𝔖1\mathfrak{S}_{1}\setminus\mathfrak{S}_{0}=\mathfrak{S}_{1} is the set of separable states. For any such state ω\omega we have

ω=∑iπiωi,{ωi}⊂extr𝔖(ℋ⊗𝒦),⇒SR(ωi)=+∞∀i.\omega=\sum_{i}\pi_{i}\omega_{i},\quad\{\omega_{i}\}\subset\mathrm{extr}\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{K}),\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad\mathrm{SR}(\omega_{i})=+\infty\quad\forall i.

C) An arbitrary pure state in 𝔖k∖𝔖k−1\;\mathfrak{S}_{k}\setminus\mathfrak{S}_{k-1}\, can be approximated by states in 𝔖k∖𝔖k−1\;\mathfrak{S}_{k}\setminus\mathfrak{S}_{k-1}\, having the property stated in B).

Proof. The first assertion directly follows from Proposition 3, the second one – from the example in the Appendix 6.2 (after Proposition 6.2).

The third assertion can be derived from the construction in the example in the Appendix 6.2 by noting that functions with non-vanishing Fourier coefficients form a dense subset in L2​([0,2​π))L^{2}([0,2\pi)) and that an arbitrary set {|ψi⟩}i=1k\{|\psi_{i}\rangle\}_{i=1}^{k} of orthogonal unit vectors in a separable Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H} can be represented as an image of the set {|φi⟩⊗|i⟩}i=1k⊂L2​([0,2​π))⊗𝒦\{|\varphi_{i}\rangle\otimes|i\rangle\}_{i=1}^{k}\subset L^{2}([0,2\pi))\otimes\mathcal{K} under some unitary map from L2​([0,2​π))⊗𝒦L^{2}([0,2\pi))\otimes\mathcal{K} onto ℋ\mathcal{H}, where {|i⟩}i=1k\{|i\rangle\}_{i=1}^{k} is an orthonormal basis in the space 𝒦\mathcal{K}. □\square

Consider the characterization of the set 𝔖k\mathfrak{S}_{k} in term of kk-positive maps (generalizing Theorem 1 in [18] to the infinite-dimensional case).

Proposition 4. A state ω∈𝔖⁡(ℋ⊗𝒦)\omega\in\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{K}) belongs to the set 𝔖k\,\mathfrak{S}_{k} if and only if the operator Λk⊗Id𝒦​(ω)\Lambda_{k}\otimes\mathrm{Id}_{\mathcal{K}}(\omega) is positive for any kk-positive linear transformation Λk\,\Lambda_{k} of the space 𝔗⁡(ℋ)\,\mathfrak{T}(\mathcal{H}).

Proof. Let ω0∈𝔖k\,\omega_{0}\in\mathfrak{S}_{k}. By Proposition 4 there exists a measure μ0\,\mu_{0} in 𝒫⁡(𝔖kp)\mathcal{P}(\mathfrak{S}^{p}_{k}) such that ω0=∫ω​μ0​(𝑑ω)\,\omega_{0}=\int\omega\mu_{0}(d\omega). Since Λk⊗Id𝒦​(ω)≥0\,\Lambda_{k}\otimes\mathrm{Id}_{\mathcal{K}}(\omega)\geq 0\, for any ω∈𝔖kp\omega\in\mathfrak{S}^{p}_{k} by definition of kk-positivity, Λk⊗Id𝒦​(ω0)=∫Λk⊗Id𝒦​(ω)​μ0​(𝑑ω)≥0\,\Lambda_{k}\otimes\mathrm{Id}_{\mathcal{K}}(\omega_{0})=\int\Lambda_{k}\otimes\mathrm{Id}_{\mathcal{K}}(\omega)\mu_{0}(d\omega)\geq 0.

The converse assertion can be derived from the corresponding finite dimensional result ([18, Theorem 1]) by using the approximation based on Lemma 3.

Let ω0∈𝔖⁡(ℋ⊗𝒦)∖𝔖k\omega_{0}\in\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{K})\setminus\mathfrak{S}_{k}, i.e. SN⁡(ω0)>k\mathrm{SN}(\omega_{0})>k. By Lemma 3 there exist projectors P∈𝔅⁡(ℋ)P\in\mathfrak{B}(\mathcal{H}) and Q∈𝔅⁡(𝒦)Q\in\mathfrak{B}(\mathcal{K}) of the same finite rank such that the state ω∗=(Tr​P⊗Q⋅ω0)−1​P⊗Q⋅ω0⋅P⊗Q\omega_{*}=(\mathrm{Tr}P\otimes Q\cdot\omega_{0})^{-1}P\otimes Q\cdot\omega_{0}\cdot P\otimes Q does not belong to the set 𝔖k\mathfrak{S}_{k}. Let ℋ∗=P⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{H}_{*}=P(\mathcal{H}) and 𝒦∗=Q⁡(𝒦)\mathcal{K}_{*}=Q(\mathcal{K}). By Theorem 1 in [18] there exists a kk-positive map Λk:𝔗⁡(ℋ∗)→𝔗⁡(ℋ∗)\Lambda_{k}:\mathfrak{T}(\mathcal{H}_{*})\rightarrow\mathfrak{T}(\mathcal{H}_{*}) such that the operator Λk⊗Id𝒦∗​(ω∗)\Lambda_{k}\otimes\mathrm{Id}_{\mathcal{K}_{*}}(\omega_{*}) is not positive. Consider the kk-positive map Λk∘Π\Lambda_{k}\circ\Pi, where Π⁡(⋅)=P⁡(⋅)​P\Pi(\cdot)=P(\cdot)P. Then the operator (Λk∘Π)⊗Id𝒦​(ω0)(\Lambda_{k}\circ\Pi)\otimes\mathrm{Id}_{\mathcal{K}}(\omega_{0}) is not positive, since otherwise the operator

Iℋ⊗Q⋅(Λk∘Π)⊗Id𝒦​(ω0)⋅Iℋ⊗Q=(Tr​P⊗Q⋅ω0)​Λk⊗Id𝒦∗​(ω∗)I_{\mathcal{H}}\otimes Q\cdot(\Lambda_{k}\circ\Pi)\otimes\mathrm{Id}_{\mathcal{K}}(\omega_{0})\cdot I_{\mathcal{H}}\otimes Q=(\mathrm{Tr}P\otimes Q\cdot\omega_{0})\,\Lambda_{k}\otimes\mathrm{Id}_{\mathcal{K}_{*}}(\omega_{*})

is positive in contradiction to the choice of Λk\Lambda_{k}. □\square

By using the compactness criterion for subsets of 𝔗+​(ℋ⊗𝒦)\mathfrak{T}_{+}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{K}) (see the Proposition in the Appendix in [6]) one can generalize Proposition 1 in [12] to infinite dimensions.

Proposition 5. An arbitrary state ωk∈𝔖k\omega_{k}\in\mathfrak{S}_{k} can be represented as follows

ωk=(1−p)​ωk−1+p​δ,p∈[0,1],\omega_{k}=(1-p)\omega_{k-1}+p\delta,\quad p\in[0,1], (4)

where ωk−1∈𝔖k−1\omega_{k-1}\in\mathfrak{S}_{k-1} and δ\delta is a state having the Schmidt number ≥k\geq k such that the operator δ−λ​σ\,\delta-\lambda\sigma is not positive for any λ>0\,\lambda>0 and any σ∈𝔖k−1\,\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{k-1}.

Among all such decompositions there is a decomposition with minimal p\,p.

A state having the property of the state δ\delta is called kk-edge state in [12]. In contrast to the finite dimensional case, to prove that δ\delta is a kk-edge state it is not sufficient to show that δ−λ​σ\,\delta-\lambda\sigma is not positive for any λ>0\,\lambda>0 and any σ∈𝔖k−1p\,\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}^{p}_{k-1}. This follows form Proposition 4B.

Proof. Let ℳ={0}∪{A∈𝔗+(ℋ⊗𝒦)|A≤ωk,(TrA)−1A∈𝔖k−1}\mathcal{M}=\{0\}\cup\{A\in\mathfrak{T}_{+}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{K})\,|\,A\leq\omega_{k},(\mathrm{Tr}A)^{-1}A\in\mathfrak{S}_{k-1}\} be a closed subset of the cone 𝔗+​(ℋ⊗𝒦)\mathfrak{T}_{+}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{K}).

Assume ℳ≠{0}\mathcal{M}\neq\{0\}. By the above-mentioned compactness criterion for subsets of 𝔗+​(ℋ⊗𝒦)\mathfrak{T}_{+}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{K}) the set ℳ\mathcal{M} is compact. Hence there exists A0∈ℳA_{0}\in\mathcal{M} such that Tr​A0=supA∈ℳTr​A\mathrm{Tr}A_{0}=\sup_{A\in\mathcal{M}}\mathrm{Tr}A. Denoting p=1−Tr​A0p=1-\mathrm{Tr}A_{0}, ωk−1=(Tr​A0)−1​A0\omega_{k-1}=(\mathrm{Tr}A_{0})^{-1}A_{0} and δ=p−1​(ωk−A0)\delta=p^{-1}(\omega_{k}-A_{0}) we obtain (4) with minimal pp.

If ℳ={0}\mathcal{M}=\{0\} then the only way to obtain (4) is to take p=1p=1 and δ=ωk\delta=\omega_{k}. □\square

Since the family {𝔖k}\{\mathfrak{S}_{k}\} consists of closed convex subsets of the Banach space 𝔗h​(ℋ⊗𝒦)\mathfrak{T}_{h}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{K}) of all trace class Hermitian operators in ℋ⊗𝒦\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{K}, for each kk and each ω0∈𝔖k∖𝔖k−1\omega_{0}\in\mathfrak{S}_{k}\setminus\mathfrak{S}_{k-1} the Hahn-Banach theorem implies existence of a Hermitian operator WW such that Tr​W​ω≥0\mathrm{Tr}W\omega\geq 0 for all ω∈𝔖k−1\omega\in\mathfrak{S}_{k-1} and Tr​W​ω0<0\mathrm{Tr}W\omega_{0}<0. This operator WW is called kk-Schmidt witness (kk-SW) detecting ω0\omega_{0} [12].

An explicit form of kk-SW detecting a state δ\delta such that the operator δ−λ​σ\,\delta-\lambda\sigma is not positive for any λ>0\,\lambda>0 and σ∈𝔖k−1\,\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{k-1} (in particular, the kk-edge state δ\delta in decomposition (4)) is given in [12, Lemma 1] (in finite dimensions). This is the operator

W=P−εc​C,W=P-\frac{\varepsilon}{c}C,

where PP is an arbitrary positive operator whose range coincides with the kernel of the state δ\delta, CC is an arbitrary positive operator such that Tr​C​δ>0\mathrm{Tr}C\delta>0, ε=inf|φ⟩​⟨φ|∈𝔖k−1p⟨φ|P|φ⟩\varepsilon=\inf_{|\varphi\rangle\langle\varphi|\in\mathfrak{S}^{p}_{k-1}}\langle\varphi|P|\varphi\rangle and c=‖C‖c=\|C\| (compactness arguments imply ε>0\varepsilon>0).

To apply the above construction in infinite dimensions we have to impose additional conditions ensuring positivity of ε\varepsilon.

Proposition 6. The above construction of kk-SW detecting the kk-edge state δ\delta is valid in infinite dimensions if the state δ\delta has finite rank and the spectrum of the operator PP does not contain zero.

Proof. By Proposition 4A to prove this assertion it suffices to show that ε=inf|φ⟩​⟨φ|∈𝔖k−1p⟨φ|P|φ⟩>0\varepsilon=\inf_{|\varphi\rangle\langle\varphi|\in\mathfrak{S}^{p}_{k-1}}\langle\varphi|P|\varphi\rangle>0 if PP is the projector on the kernel of δ\delta.

Assume that ε=0\varepsilon=0. Then there exists a sequence {|φn⟩}\{|\varphi_{n}\rangle\} of vectors such that |φn⟩​⟨φn|∈𝔖k−1p|\varphi_{n}\rangle\langle\varphi_{n}|\in\mathfrak{S}^{p}_{k-1} for each nn and limn→+∞⟨φn|Iℋ⊗𝒦−P|φn⟩=1\lim_{n\rightarrow+\infty}\langle\varphi_{n}|I_{\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{K}}-P|\varphi_{n}\rangle=1. The weak compactness of the unit ball of ℋ⊗𝒦\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{K} implies existence of a subsequence {|φnk⟩}\{|\varphi_{n_{k}}\rangle\} weakly converging to a vector |φ∗⟩|\varphi_{*}\rangle. Since Iℋ⊗𝒦−PI_{\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{K}}-P is a finite rank projector, we have

⟨φ∗|Iℋ⊗𝒦−P|φ∗⟩=limn→+∞⟨φn|Iℋ⊗𝒦−P|φn⟩=1.\langle\varphi_{*}|I_{\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{K}}-P|\varphi_{*}\rangle=\lim_{n\rightarrow+\infty}\langle\varphi_{n}|I_{\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{K}}-P|\varphi_{n}\rangle=1.

Thus |φ∗⟩|\varphi_{*}\rangle is a unit vector belonging to the range of δ\delta and hence the subsequence {|φnk⟩}\{|\varphi_{n_{k}}\rangle\} converges to the vector |φ∗⟩|\varphi_{*}\rangle in the norm topology. This implies |φ∗⟩​⟨φ∗|∈𝔖k−1p|\varphi_{*}\rangle\langle\varphi_{*}|\in\mathfrak{S}^{p}_{k-1} contradicting to the basic property of the state δ\delta. □\square

5 Partially entanglement breaking channels

The notion of a kk-partially entanglement-breaking (kk-PEB) channel in finite dimensions is introduced in [3] as a natural generalization of the notion of an entanglement-breaking channel (which is 11-PEB). According to [3], a channel Φ:𝔗⁡(ℋ)→𝔗⁡(ℋ′)\,\Phi:\mathfrak{T}(\mathcal{H})\rightarrow\mathfrak{T}(\mathcal{H}^{\prime}) is called kk-partially entanglement-breaking if for an arbitrary Hilbert space 𝒦\mathcal{K} the Schmidt number of the state Φ⊗Id𝒦​(ω)∈𝔖⁡(ℋ′⊗𝒦)\,\Phi\otimes\mathrm{Id}_{\mathcal{K}}(\omega)\in\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}^{\prime}\otimes\mathcal{K}) does not exceed kk for any state ω∈𝔖⁡(ℋ⊗𝒦)\omega\in\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{K}).

By using the definition of the Schmidt number introduced in Section 3 the above definition of kk-partially entanglement breaking channels is directly generalized to the infinite-dimensional case.

Denote by 𝔓k​(ℋ,ℋ′)\mathfrak{P}_{k}(\mathcal{H},\mathcal{H}^{\prime}) the class of kk-partially entanglement breaking channels from 𝔗⁡(ℋ)\mathfrak{T}(\mathcal{H}) to 𝔗⁡(ℋ′)\mathfrak{T}(\mathcal{H}^{\prime}). Since the set 𝔖k​(ℋ′⊗𝒦)\mathfrak{S}_{k}(\mathcal{H}^{\prime}\otimes\mathcal{K}) is closed and convex, 𝔓k​(ℋ,ℋ′)\mathfrak{P}_{k}(\mathcal{H},\mathcal{H}^{\prime}) is a closed convex subset of the set 𝔉⁡(ℋ,ℋ′)\mathfrak{F}(\mathcal{H},\mathcal{H}^{\prime}) of all channels from 𝔗⁡(ℋ)\mathfrak{T}(\mathcal{H}) to 𝔗⁡(ℋ′)\mathfrak{T}(\mathcal{H}^{\prime}) endowed with the strong convergence topology [6].

Proposition 4 implies the following characterization of kk-PEB channels (generalizing the corresponding finite-dimensional results [3, 7]).

Proposition 7. A channel Φ\,\Phi is kk-partially entanglement breaking if and only if the map Λk∘Φ\Lambda_{k}\circ\Phi is completely positive for any kk-positive map Λk\Lambda_{k}.

By definition Φ∈𝔓k​(ℋ,ℋ′)\Phi\in\mathfrak{P}_{k}(\mathcal{H},\mathcal{H}^{\prime}) means that Φ⊗Id𝒦​(ω)∈𝔖k​(ℋ′⊗𝒦)\Phi\otimes\mathrm{Id}_{\mathcal{K}}(\omega)\in\mathfrak{S}_{k}(\mathcal{H}^{\prime}\otimes\mathcal{K}) for any ω∈𝔖⁡(ℋ⊗𝒦)\omega\in\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{K}). By the following proposition it suffices to verify the above inclusion only for one pure state.

Proposition 8. Let Φ:𝔗⁡(ℋ)→𝔗⁡(ℋ′)\,\Phi:\mathfrak{T}(\mathcal{H})\rightarrow\mathfrak{T}(\mathcal{H}^{\prime}) be a quantum channel. If there exists a pure state |ψ⟩​⟨ψ||\psi\rangle\langle\psi| in 𝔖⁡(ℋ⊗𝒦)\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{K}) having full rank partial states Tr𝒦​|ψ⟩​⟨ψ|≅Trℋ​|ψ⟩​⟨ψ|\mathrm{Tr}_{\mathcal{K}}|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|\cong\mathrm{Tr}_{\mathcal{H}}|\psi\rangle\langle\psi| such that Φ⊗Id𝒦​(|ψ⟩​⟨ψ|)∈𝔖k​(ℋ′⊗𝒦)\,\Phi\otimes\mathrm{Id}_{\mathcal{K}}(|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|)\in\mathfrak{S}_{k}(\mathcal{H}^{\prime}\otimes\mathcal{K}) then the channel Φ\,\Phi is kk-partially entanglement-breaking.

Proof. Let |ψ⟩=∑i=1+∞μi​|i⟩⊗|i⟩|\psi\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^{+\infty}\mu_{i}|i\rangle\otimes|i\rangle, where {|i⟩}\{|i\rangle\} is an orthonormal basis in ℋ≅𝒦\mathcal{H}\cong\mathcal{K} and μi>0\mu_{i}>0 for all ii. Let Pn=∑i=1n|i⟩​⟨i|P_{n}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}|i\rangle\langle i|\, be a projector in 𝔅⁡(𝒦)\mathfrak{B}(\mathcal{K}).

By Proposition 3 we have

Φ⊗Id𝒦​(|ψn⟩​⟨ψn|)=cn​Iℋ⊗Pn⋅Φ⊗Id𝒦​(|ψ⟩​⟨ψ|)⋅Iℋ⊗Pn∈𝔖k​(ℋ′⊗𝒦)\Phi\otimes\mathrm{Id}_{\mathcal{K}}(|\psi_{n}\rangle\langle\psi_{n}|)=c_{n}I_{\mathcal{H}}\otimes P_{n}\cdot\Phi\otimes\mathrm{Id}_{\mathcal{K}}(|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|)\cdot I_{\mathcal{H}}\otimes P_{n}\in\mathfrak{S}_{k}(\mathcal{H}^{\prime}\otimes\mathcal{K})

where |ψn⟩=cn​∑i=1nμi​|i⟩⊗|i⟩|\psi_{n}\rangle=c_{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mu_{i}|i\rangle\otimes|i\rangle and cn=[∑i=1nμi2]−1/2c_{n}=[\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mu_{i}^{2}]^{-1/2}.

Let ℋn=lin⁡({|i⟩}i=1n)\mathcal{H}_{n}=\mathrm{lin}(\{|i\rangle\}_{i=1}^{n}) and 𝒦n=lin⁡({|i⟩}i=1n)\mathcal{K}_{n}=\mathrm{lin}(\{|i\rangle\}_{i=1}^{n}) be nn-dimensional subspaces of ℋ\mathcal{H} and 𝒦\mathcal{K}. An arbitrary vector |φ⟩|\varphi\rangle in ℋn⊗𝒦n\mathcal{H}_{n}\otimes\mathcal{K}_{n} can be represented as follows |φ⟩=∑i,j=1nγi​j​|i⟩⊗|j⟩=∑i=1nμi​|i⟩⊗A⁡|i⟩|\varphi\rangle=\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}\gamma_{ij}|i\rangle\otimes|j\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mu_{i}|i\rangle\otimes A|i\rangle, where A=∑i,j=1n(μi)−1​γi​j​|j⟩​⟨i|A=\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}(\mu_{i})^{-1}\gamma_{ij}|j\rangle\langle i| is an operator in 𝔅⁡(𝒦n)\mathfrak{B}(\mathcal{K}_{n}). Thus |φ⟩​⟨φ|=Iℋn⊗A⋅|ψn⟩​⟨ψn|⋅Iℋn⊗A∗|\varphi\rangle\langle\varphi|=I_{\mathcal{H}_{n}}\otimes A\cdot|\psi_{n}\rangle\langle\psi_{n}|\cdot I_{\mathcal{H}_{n}}\otimes A^{*} and hence

Φ⊗Id𝒦​(|φ⟩​⟨φ|)=Iℋ⊗A⋅Φ⊗Id𝒦​(|ψn⟩​⟨ψn|)⋅Iℋ⊗A∗∈𝔖k​(ℋ′⊗𝒦).\Phi\otimes\mathrm{Id}_{\mathcal{K}}(|\varphi\rangle\langle\varphi|)=I_{\mathcal{H}}\otimes A\cdot\Phi\otimes\mathrm{Id}_{\mathcal{K}}(|\psi_{n}\rangle\langle\psi_{n}|)\cdot I_{\mathcal{H}}\otimes A^{*}\in\mathfrak{S}_{k}(\mathcal{H}^{\prime}\otimes\mathcal{K}).

This means that the restriction of the channel Φ\,\Phi to the set 𝔖⁡(ℋn)\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}_{n}) is kk-partially entanglement breaking. By the below Lemma 5 the channel Φ\,\Phi is kk-partially entanglement breaking. □\square

The following lemma reduces a proof of the kk-partially entanglement breaking property of a channel Φ:𝔗⁡(ℋ)→𝔗⁡(ℋ′)\,\Phi:\mathfrak{T}(\mathcal{H})\rightarrow\mathfrak{T}(\mathcal{H}^{\prime})\, to analysis of its finite-dimensional restrictions.

Lemma 2. Let {ℋn}\{\mathcal{H}_{n}\} be an increasing sequence of subspaces of ℋ\mathcal{H} such that cl⁡(⋃nℋn)=ℋ\,\mathrm{cl}(\bigcup_{n}\mathcal{H}_{n})=\mathcal{H}. If the restriction of the channel Φ\,\Phi to the set 𝔖⁡(ℋn)\,\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}_{n}) is kk-partially entanglement breaking for each n\,n\, then the channel Φ\,\Phi is kk-partially entanglement breaking.

Proof. Since an arbitrary state ω∈𝔖⁡(ℋ⊗𝒦)\omega\in\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{K}) can be approximated by a sequence {ωn}\{\omega_{n}\} such that suppTr𝒦​ωn⊂ℋn\mathrm{supp}\mathrm{Tr}_{\mathcal{K}}\omega_{n}\subset\mathcal{H}_{n} (see Lemma 3), this assertion follows from closedness of the set 𝔖k​(ℋ′⊗𝒦)\mathfrak{S}_{k}(\mathcal{H}^{\prime}\otimes\mathcal{K}). □\square

Let |ψ⟩​⟨ψ||\psi\rangle\langle\psi| be a pure state in 𝔖⁡(ℋ⊗𝒦)\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{K}) having full rank partial states Tr𝒦​|ψ⟩​⟨ψ|≅Trℋ​|ψ⟩​⟨ψ|=σ\mathrm{Tr}_{\mathcal{K}}|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|\cong\mathrm{Tr}_{\mathcal{H}}|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|=\sigma. Consider the Choi-Jamiolkowski one-to-one correspondence

𝔉⁡(ℋ,ℋ′)∋Φ↔Φ⊗Id𝒦​(|ψ⟩​⟨ψ|)∈ℭσ≐{ω∈𝔖⁡(ℋ′⊗𝒦)|Trℋ′​ω=σ},\mathfrak{F}(\mathcal{H},\mathcal{H}^{\prime})\ni\Phi\leftrightarrow\Phi\otimes\mathrm{Id}_{\mathcal{K}}(|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|)\in\mathfrak{C}_{\sigma}\doteq\{\omega\in\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}^{\prime}\otimes\mathcal{K})\,|\,\mathrm{Tr}_{\mathcal{H}^{\prime}}\omega=\sigma\},

which is a topological isomorphism provided the set 𝔉⁡(ℋ,ℋ′)\mathfrak{F}(\mathcal{H},\mathcal{H}^{\prime}) of all channels is endowed with the strong convergence topology [6, Proposition 3]. Proposition 5 implies the following observation.

Corollary 1. The restriction of the Choi-Jamiolkowski isomorphism to the class 𝔓k​(ℋ,ℋ′)\,\mathfrak{P}_{k}(\mathcal{H},\mathcal{H}^{\prime}) is an isomorphism between this class and the closed subset 𝔖k​(ℋ′⊗𝒦)∩ℭσ\,\mathfrak{S}_{k}(\mathcal{H}^{\prime}\otimes\mathcal{K})\cap\mathfrak{C}_{\sigma} of the set 𝔖⁡(ℋ′⊗𝒦)\,\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}^{\prime}\otimes\mathcal{K}).

The set 𝔓k​(ℋ,ℋ′)∖𝔓k−1​(ℋ,ℋ′)\,\mathfrak{P}_{k}(\mathcal{H},\mathcal{H}^{\prime})\setminus\mathfrak{P}_{k-1}(\mathcal{H},\mathcal{H}^{\prime}) corresponds to the set

(𝔖k​(ℋ′⊗𝒦)∖𝔖k−1​(ℋ′⊗𝒦))∩ℭσ,k=2,3,…(\mathfrak{S}_{k}(\mathcal{H}^{\prime}\otimes\mathcal{K})\setminus\mathfrak{S}_{k-1}(\mathcal{H}^{\prime}\otimes\mathcal{K}))\cap\mathfrak{C}_{\sigma},\quad k=2,3,...

under this isomorphism.

In [3] it is proved that a channel Φ\Phi is kk-PEB if and only if it has the Kraus representation

Φ⁡(⋅)=∑iVi​(⋅)​Vi∗\Phi(\cdot)=\sum_{i}V_{i}(\cdot)V_{i}^{*} (5)

such that rank​Vi≤k\mathrm{rank}V_{i}\leq k for all i\,i (this is a natural generalization of the well known characterization of entanglement breaking finite-dimensional channels proved in [7]). In infinite dimensions the class of kk-PEB channels is wider than the class of channels having the last property.

Proposition 9. A) A channel Φ\,\Phi belongs to the class 𝔓k​(ℋ,ℋ′)\,\mathfrak{P}_{k}(\mathcal{H},\mathcal{H}^{\prime}) if it has the Kraus representation (5) such that rank​Vi≤k\,\mathrm{rank}V_{i}\leq k\, for all i\,i.

B) There exist channels Φ\,\Phi in 𝔓k​(ℋ,ℋ′)∖𝔓k−1​(ℋ,ℋ′)\;\mathfrak{P}_{k}(\mathcal{H},\mathcal{H}^{\prime})\setminus\mathfrak{P}_{k-1}(\mathcal{H},\mathcal{H}^{\prime})\, with the following property44 4 It is assumed that 𝔓0​(ℋ,ℋ′)=∅\mathfrak{P}_{0}(\mathcal{H},\mathcal{H}^{\prime})=\emptyset, so that 𝔓1​(ℋ,ℋ′)∖𝔓0​(ℋ,ℋ′)=𝔓1​(ℋ,ℋ′)\mathfrak{P}_{1}(\mathcal{H},\mathcal{H}^{\prime})\setminus\mathfrak{P}_{0}(\mathcal{H},\mathcal{H}^{\prime})=\mathfrak{P}_{1}(\mathcal{H},\mathcal{H}^{\prime}) is the class of entanglement breaking channels.

Φ⁡(⋅)=∑iVi​(⋅)​Vi∗⇒rank​Vi=+∞∀i.\Phi(\cdot)=\sum_{i}V_{i}(\cdot)V_{i}^{*}\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad\mathrm{rank}V_{i}=+\infty\quad\forall\,i.

Proof. The first assertion is obvious, since for an arbitrary pure state ω∈𝔖⁡(ℋ⊗𝒦)\omega\in\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{K}) the expression Φ⊗Id𝒦​(ω)=∑iVi⊗I𝒦⋅ω⋅Vi∗⊗I𝒦\Phi\otimes\mathrm{Id}_{\mathcal{K}}(\omega)=\sum_{i}V_{i}\otimes I_{\mathcal{K}}\cdot\omega\cdot V_{i}^{*}\otimes I_{\mathcal{K}} gives a decomposition of the state Φ⊗Id𝒦​(ω)\Phi\otimes\mathrm{Id}_{\mathcal{K}}(\omega) into a convex combination of pure states with the Schmidt rank ≤k\leq k.

To prove the second one consider a state ω\,\omega in 𝔖k​(ℋ′⊗𝒦)∖𝔖k−1​(ℋ′⊗𝒦)\mathfrak{S}_{k}(\mathcal{H}^{\prime}\otimes\mathcal{K})\setminus\mathfrak{S}_{k-1}(\mathcal{H}^{\prime}\otimes\mathcal{K}) having the property stated in Proposition 4B. We may assume that Trℋ′​ω\mathrm{Tr}_{\mathcal{H}^{\prime}}\omega is a full rank state in 𝔖⁡(𝒦)\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{K}). Let |ψ⟩​⟨ψ||\psi\rangle\langle\psi| be a purification of this state in 𝔖⁡(ℋ⊗𝒦)\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{K}). By Corollary 5 the channel Φω\Phi_{\omega} corresponding to the state ω\,\omega via the Choi-Jamiolkowski isomorphism induced by the state |ψ⟩​⟨ψ||\psi\rangle\langle\psi| belongs to the set 𝔓k​(ℋ,ℋ′)∖𝔓k−1​(ℋ,ℋ′)\mathfrak{P}_{k}(\mathcal{H},\mathcal{H}^{\prime})\setminus\mathfrak{P}_{k-1}(\mathcal{H},\mathcal{H}^{\prime}). If we assume that Φω​(⋅)=∑iVi​(⋅)​Vi∗\Phi_{\omega}(\cdot)=\sum_{i}V_{i}(\cdot)V_{i}^{*} with rank​Vi0<+∞\mathrm{rank}V_{i_{0}}<+\infty for some i0i_{0} then we will obtain a contradiction to the property of the state ω\,\omega, since Vi0⊗Id𝒦​|ψ⟩≠0V_{i_{0}}\otimes\mathrm{Id}_{\mathcal{K}}|\psi\rangle\neq 0 (otherwise Vi0​(Tr𝒦​|ψ⟩​⟨ψ|)​(Vi0)∗=0V_{i_{0}}(\mathrm{Tr}_{\mathcal{K}}|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|)(V_{i_{0}})^{*}=0 contradicting to a full rank of the state Tr𝒦​|ψ⟩​⟨ψ|\mathrm{Tr}_{\mathcal{K}}|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|). □\square

Corollary 2. There exist entanglement breaking channels such that all operators in any their Kraus representations have infinite rank.

6 Appendix

6.1 One property of the set 𝔖⁡(ℋ)\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}).

We consider here a corollary of the compactness criterion for subsets of probability measures on the set 𝔖⁡(ℋ)\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}) (described in detail in [13, Section 1]), which states that a subset 𝒫\mathcal{P} of 𝒫⁡(𝔖⁡(ℋ))\mathcal{P}(\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H})) is compact (in the weak convergence topology) if and only if {b​(μ)|μ∈𝒫}\,\{\textbf{b}(\mu)\,|\,\mu\in\mathcal{P}\} is a compact subset of 𝔖⁡(ℋ)\,\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}) .

Proposition 10. Let ff be a nonnegative lower-semicontinuous function on a closed subset 𝒜\mathcal{A} of 𝔖⁡(ℋ)\,\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}). The function

F⁡(ρ)=infμ∈𝒫{ρ}​(𝒜)ess​supμ​f​(⋅)F(\rho)=\inf_{\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{\{\rho\}}(\mathcal{A})}\mathrm{ess}\,\mathrm{sup}_{\mu}f(\cdot) (6)

is lower semicontinuous on the set co¯​(𝒜)\,\overline{\mathrm{co}}(\mathcal{A}).55 5 "​ess​supμ​""\mathrm{ess}\,\mathrm{sup}_{\mu}" means the essential supremum with respect to the measure μ\mu [1, Sec.13.1]. For each state ρ∈co¯​(𝒜)\,\rho\in\overline{\mathrm{co}}(\mathcal{A}) the infimum in (6) is achieved at some measure in extr​𝒫{ρ}​(𝒜)\,\mathrm{extr}\mathcal{P}_{\{\rho\}}(\mathcal{A}).

For each c≥0c\geq 0 the set {ρ∈co¯​(𝒜)|F⁡(ρ)≤c}\,\{\rho\in\overline{\mathrm{co}}(\mathcal{A})\,|\,F(\rho)\leq c\} coincides with the convex closure of the set {ρ∈𝒜|f⁡(ρ)≤c}\,\{\rho\in\mathcal{A}\,|\,f(\rho)\leq c\}.

Proof. Note first that the function F⁡(ρ)F(\rho) is well defined on the set co¯​(𝒜)\,\overline{\mathrm{co}}(\mathcal{A}) by Lemma 1 in [5].

Show that the functional

𝒫⁡(𝒜)∋μ↦f^​(μ)=ess​supμ​f​(⋅)\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{A})\ni\mu\mapsto\hat{f}(\mu)=\mathrm{ess}\,\mathrm{sup}_{\mu}f(\cdot) (7)

is concave and lower semicontinuous. Since for a given measure μ∈𝒫⁡(𝒜)\mu\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{A}) the μ\mu-essential supremum of the function ff (coinciding with the norm ‖f‖∞\|f\|_{\infty} in the space L∞​(𝒜,μ)L^{\infty}(\mathcal{A},\mu)) is the least upper bound of the increasing family of the norms ‖f‖p\|f\|_{p} in the space Lp​(𝒜,μ)L^{p}(\mathcal{A},\mu), p∈[1,+∞)p\in[1,+\infty), concavity and lower semicontinuity of functional (7) follow from concavity and lower semicontinuity of the functional

𝒫⁡(𝒜)∋μ↦‖f‖p=∫𝒜[f⁡(ρ)]p​μ​(𝑑ρ)p\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{A})\ni\mu\mapsto\|f\|_{p}=\sqrt[p]{\int_{\mathcal{A}}[f(\rho)]^{p}\mu(d\rho)}

(lower semicontinuity of this functional follows from the basic properties of the weak convergence topology, see [2, Chapter I, Sec.2]).

By concavity and lower semicontinuity of functional (7) and compactness of the set 𝒫{ρ}​(𝒜)\mathcal{P}_{\{\rho\}}(\mathcal{A}) (provided by the above-stated compactness criterion) the infimum in the definition of the value F⁡(ρ)F(\rho) for each ρ\rho in co¯​(𝒜)\overline{\mathrm{co}}(\mathcal{A}) is achieved at a particular measure in extr​𝒫{ρ}​(𝒜)\mathrm{extr}\mathcal{P}_{\{\rho\}}(\mathcal{A}).

Suppose function (6) is not lower semicontinuous. Then there exists a sequence {ρn}⊂co¯​(𝒜)\{\rho_{n}\}\subset\overline{\mathrm{co}}(\mathcal{A}) converging to a state ρ0∈co¯​(𝒜)\rho_{0}\in\overline{\mathrm{co}}(\mathcal{A}) such that

By continuity of the map μ↦𝐛⁡(μ)\mu\mapsto\mathbf{b}(\mu) the measure μ0\mu_{0} belongs to the set 𝒫{ρ0}​(𝒜)\mathcal{P}_{\{\rho_{0}\}}(\mathcal{A}). Lower semicontinuity of functional (7) implies

contradicting to (8).

The last assertion of the proposition follows from the previous ones and Lemma 1 in [5]. □\square

6.2 Existence of a state with a given finite Schmidt number such that any its countable convex decomposition does not contain pure states with a finite Schmidt rank

In this section we show first that the separable non-countably decomposable state constructed in [5] has, in fact, more stronger property: any countable decomposition of this state does not contain pure states with finite Schmidt rank (non-countable decomposability means nonexistence of such decomposition into product pure states – states with the Schmidt rank =1=1). By using this observation we construct a state with a given finite Schmidt number such that any countable decomposition of this state does not contain pure states with a finite Schmidt rank.

We present the construction of the above mentioned separable state following the notations of [5]. Consider the one-dimensional rotation group represented as the interval [0,2​π)[0,2\pi) with addition mod2​π.2\pi. Let ℋ=L2​([0,2​π))\mathcal{H=}L^{2}([0,2\pi)) with the normalized Lebesgue measure d​x2​π,\frac{dx}{2\pi}, and let {|k⟩;k∈𝐙}\left\{|k\rangle;k\in\mathbf{Z}\right\} be the orthonormal basis of trigonometric functions, so that

⟨k|ψ⟩=∫02​πe−i​x​k​ψ​(x)​d​x2​π.\langle k|\psi\rangle=\int_{0}^{2\pi}e^{-ixk}\psi(x)\frac{dx}{2\pi}.

Consider the unitary representation x→Vx\,x\rightarrow V_{x} , where Vx=∑−∞+∞ei​x​k​|k⟩​⟨k|,V_{x}=\sum_{-\infty}^{+\infty}e^{ixk}|k\rangle\langle k|, so that (Vu​ψ)​(x)=ψ⁡(x+u)(V_{u}\psi)(x)=\psi(x+u).

For arbitrary unit vectors |φj⟩∈ℋj≃L2([0,2π)),j=1,2,|\varphi_{j}\rangle\in\mathcal{H}_{j}\simeq L^{2}([0,2\pi)),j=1,2, consider the separable state

ρ12=∫02​πVx(1)​|φ1⟩​⟨φ1|(Vx(1))∗⊗Vx(2)|φ2⟩​⟨φ2|​(Vx(2))∗​d​x2​π.\rho_{12}=\int_{0}^{2\pi}V_{x}^{(1)}|\varphi_{1}\rangle\langle\varphi_{1}|(V_{x}^{(1)})^{*}\otimes V_{x}^{(2)}|\varphi_{2}\rangle\langle\varphi_{2}|(V_{x}^{(2)})^{*}\;\frac{dx}{2\pi}. (9)

.

The following proposition strengthens the assertion of Theorem 3 in [5]. It is obtained by a natural generalization of the proof of this theorem.

Proposition 11. Let ρ12\rho_{12} be the separable state defined in (9). If the vectors |φj⟩|\varphi_{j}\rangle have nonvanishing Fourier coefficients then the operator

ρ12−λ​σ\rho_{12}-\lambda\sigma

is not positive for any λ>0\lambda>0 and any pure state σ\sigma with finite Schmidt rank.

It follows that any countable decomposition of the state ρ12\rho_{12} does not contain pure states with finite Schmidt rank.

Proof. Suppose there exists a vector |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle in ℋ1⊗ℋ2\mathcal{H}_{1}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{2} with the Schmidt rank nn such that

ρ12≥|ψ⟩​⟨ψ|.\rho_{12}\geq|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|. (10)

Let |ψ⟩=∑i=1n|αi1⟩⊗|αi2⟩|\psi\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}|\alpha^{1}_{i}\rangle\otimes|\alpha^{2}_{i}\rangle, where {|αij⟩}i=1n\{|\alpha^{j}_{i}\rangle\}_{i=1}^{n}, j=1,2j=1,2, are sets of orthogonal vectors. Inequality (10) implies

∫02​π|⟨λ1|Vx(1)|φ1⟩|2​|⟨λ2|Vx(2)|φ2⟩|2​d​x2​π≥|∑i=1n⟨λ1|αi1⟩​⟨λ2|αi2⟩|2\int_{0}^{2\pi}\left|\langle\lambda_{1}|V_{x}^{(1)}|\varphi_{1}\rangle\right|^{2}\left|\langle\lambda_{2}|V_{x}^{(2)}|\varphi_{2}\rangle\right|^{2}\;\frac{dx}{2\pi}\geq\left|\sum_{i=1}^{n}\langle\lambda_{1}|\alpha^{1}_{i}\rangle\langle\lambda_{2}|\alpha^{2}_{i}\rangle\right|^{2} (11)

for arbitrary λj∈L2​([0,2​π))\lambda_{j}\in L^{2}([0,2\pi)), j=1,2j=1,2.

Consider the linear maps

L2​([0,2​π))∋λ↦Φj​(λ)={⟨αij|λ⟩}i=1n∈ℂnL^{2}([0,2\pi))\ni\lambda\mapsto\Phi_{j}(\lambda)=\{\langle\alpha^{j}_{i}|\lambda\rangle\}_{i=1}^{n}\in\mathbb{C}^{n}

and

L2([0,2π))∋λ↦Ψj(λ)=⟨λ|Vx(j)|φj⟩¯=∑k=−∞+∞⟨φj|k⟩⟨k|λ⟩e−i​k​x,j=1,2.L^{2}([0,2\pi))\ni\lambda\mapsto\Psi_{j}(\lambda)=\overline{\langle\lambda|V_{x}^{(j)}|\varphi_{j}\rangle}=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{+\infty}\langle\varphi_{j}|k\rangle\langle k|\lambda\rangle e^{-ikx},\quad j=1,2.

Let ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} be a dense subset of L2​([0,2​π))L^{2}([0,2\pi)) consisting of functions having finite number of nonzero Fourier coefficients (trigonometric polynomials). Since ⟨φj|k⟩≠0\langle\varphi_{j}|k\rangle\neq 0 for all kk, the maps Ψj\Psi_{j}, j=1,2j=1,2, are linear isomorphisms from ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} onto itself. Hence (11) implies

|⟨A1​(ξ),Ξ⁡(A2​(η))⟩ℂn|2≤∫02​π|ξ⁡(x)​η​(x)|2​d​x2​π,ξ,η∈ℋ0,|\langle A_{1}(\xi),\Xi(A_{2}(\eta))\rangle_{\mathbb{C}^{n}}|^{2}\leq\int_{0}^{2\pi}\left|\xi(x)\eta(x)\right|^{2}\;\frac{dx}{2\pi},\quad\xi,\eta\in\mathcal{H}_{0}, (12)

where Aj​(⋅)=Φj​(Ψj−1​(⋅))A_{j}(\cdot)=\Phi_{j}(\Psi^{-1}_{j}(\cdot)), j=1,2j=1,2, are linear maps from ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} to ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} and Ξ\Xi is the complex conjugation in ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}.

Since {Φ2​(λ)|λ∈L2​([0,2​π))}=ℂn\{\Phi_{2}(\lambda)\,|\,\lambda\in L^{2}([0,2\pi))\}=\mathbb{C}^{n}, we have {Φ2​(λ)|λ∈ℋ0}=ℂn\{\Phi_{2}(\lambda)\,|\,\lambda\in\mathcal{H}_{0}\}=\mathbb{C}^{n} and hence {A2​(ξ)|ξ∈ℋ0}=ℂn\{A_{2}(\xi)\,|\,\xi\in\mathcal{H}_{0}\}=\mathbb{C}^{n}. In the following lemma the linear independence of measurable functions f1,…,fn\;f_{1},...,f_{n}\, on a measurable subset 𝒜⊂ℝ\mathcal{A}\subset\mathbb{R} means that any nontrivial linear combination of these functions ≠0\neq 0 a.e. on 𝒜\mathcal{A}.

Lemma 3. Let f1,…,fn\;f_{1},...,f_{n}\, be linearly independent measurable functions on [a,b][a,b]. For arbitrary ε>0\,\varepsilon>0 there exists a subset 𝒜⊂[a,b]\mathcal{A}\subset[a,b] with the Lebesgue measure μ⁡(𝒜)<ε\mu(\mathcal{A})<\varepsilon\, such that the functions f1,…,fn\;f_{1},...,f_{n}\, are linearly independent on 𝒜\,\mathcal{A}.

Proof. For n=1,2n=1,2 the assertion of the lemma is obvious. Assume it is valid for given nn and show its validity for n+1n+1.66 6 There is an elegant proof of this lemma non-using the induction method [15].

By the assumption for arbitrary ε>0\varepsilon>0 and for each family {fi}∖fj\{f_{i}\}\setminus f_{j}, j=1,n+1¯j=\overline{1,n+1}, there exists a subset 𝒜jε⊂[a,b]\mathcal{A}^{\varepsilon}_{j}\subset[a,b] with μ⁡(𝒜jε)<ε\mu(\mathcal{A}^{\varepsilon}_{j})<\varepsilon such that the functions of the above family are linearly independent on 𝒜jε\mathcal{A}^{\varepsilon}_{j}.

If the assertion of the lemma is not valid for n+1n+1 then there exists ε∗>0\varepsilon_{*}>0\, such that the functions f1,…,fn+1\,f_{1},...,f_{n+1}\, are linearly dependent on any subset 𝒜⊂[a,b]\mathcal{A}\subset[a,b]\, with μ⁡(𝒜)<ε∗\mu(\mathcal{A})<\varepsilon_{*}.

Let ε<ε∗/2​(n+1)\varepsilon<\varepsilon_{*}/2(n+1) and 𝒜ε=⋃j=1n+1𝒜jε\mathcal{A}^{\varepsilon}=\bigcup_{j=1}^{n+1}\mathcal{A}^{\varepsilon}_{j}. Choose a finite collection {ℬk}\{\mathcal{B}_{k}\} of disjoint subsets of [a,b]∖𝒜ε[a,b]\setminus\mathcal{A}^{\varepsilon} such that μ⁡(ℬk)<ε∗/2\mu(\mathcal{B}_{k})<\varepsilon_{*}/2 and ⋃kℬk=[a,b]∖𝒜ε\bigcup_{k}\mathcal{B}_{k}=[a,b]\setminus\mathcal{A}^{\varepsilon}.

For each kk let 𝒞k=𝒜ε∪ℬk\mathcal{C}_{k}=\mathcal{A}^{\varepsilon}\cup\mathcal{B}_{k}. Since μ⁡(𝒞k)<ε∗\mu(\mathcal{C}_{k})<\varepsilon_{*} there exists a set {λik}i=1n+1\{\lambda^{k}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n+1} of complex numbers such that

∑i=1n+1λik​fi​(x)=0a.e. on​𝒞k,∑i=1n+1|λik|>0.\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}\lambda^{k}_{i}f_{i}(x)=0\quad\text{a.e. on}\;\,\mathcal{C}_{k},\quad\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}|\lambda_{i}^{k}|>0. (14)

Since 𝒜jε⊂𝒞k\mathcal{A}^{\varepsilon}_{j}\subset\mathcal{C}_{k} for all jj, it is easy to see that λik≠0\lambda^{k}_{i}\neq 0 for all ii. So, we may assume that λn+1k=1\lambda^{k}_{n+1}=1. Since the functions f1,…,fn+1\,f_{1},...,f_{n+1}\, are linearly independent on [a,b]=⋃k𝒞k[a,b]=\bigcup_{k}\mathcal{C}_{k}, there exist k1k_{1} and k2k_{2} such that {λik1}i=1n+1≠{λik2}i=1n+1\{\lambda^{k_{1}}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n+1}\neq\{\lambda^{k_{2}}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n+1}. It follows from (14) that

∑i=1n(λik1−λik2)​fi​(x)=0a.e. on​𝒜n+1ε⊆𝒞k1∩𝒞k2,∑i=1n|λik1−λik2|>0\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\lambda_{i}^{k_{1}}-\lambda_{i}^{k_{2}})f_{i}(x)=0\quad\text{a.e. on}\;\,\mathcal{A}_{n+1}^{\varepsilon}\subseteq\mathcal{C}_{k_{1}}\cap\mathcal{C}_{k_{2}},\qquad\sum_{i=1}^{n}|\lambda_{i}^{k_{1}}-\lambda_{i}^{k_{2}}|>0

contradicting to the construction of the set 𝒜n+1ε\mathcal{A}_{n+1}^{\varepsilon}. □\square

Example of a state ω\,\omega with SN⁡(ω)=k∈ℕ\,\mathrm{SN}(\omega)=k\in\mathbb{N} such that the operator ω−λ​σ\,\omega-\lambda\sigma is not positive for any pure state σ\sigma with a finite Schmidt rank and any λ>0\lambda>0.

Let {|φ1i⟩}i=1k\{|\varphi^{i}_{1}\rangle\}_{i=1}^{k} and {|φ2i⟩}i=1k\{|\varphi^{i}_{2}\rangle\}_{i=1}^{k} are collections of orthogonal unit vectors in ℋ1=L2​([0,2​π))\mathcal{H}_{1}=L^{2}([0,2\pi)) and ℋ2=L2​([0,2​π))\mathcal{H}_{2}=L^{2}([0,2\pi)) correspondingly with non-vanishing Fourier coefficients. Let 𝒦\mathcal{K} be the kk-dimensional Hilbert space with the orthonormal basis {|i⟩}i=1k\{|i\rangle\}_{i=1}^{k}. For each natural nn consider the state

ρ123n=∫02​π/nVx(1)⊗Vx(2)⊗I𝒦⋅|Ω⟩​⟨Ω|⋅(Vx(1))∗⊗(Vx(2))∗⊗I𝒦​n​d​x2​π\rho^{n}_{123}=\int_{0}^{2\pi/n}V_{x}^{(1)}\otimes V_{x}^{(2)}\otimes I_{\mathcal{K}}\,\cdot|\Omega\rangle\langle\Omega|\cdot\,(V_{x}^{(1)})^{*}\otimes(V_{x}^{(2)})^{*}\otimes I_{\mathcal{K}}\;\frac{ndx}{2\pi} (15)

in 𝔖⁡(ℋ1⊗ℋ2⊗𝒦)\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}_{1}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{2}\otimes\mathcal{K}), where |Ω⟩=1k​∑i=1k|φ1i⟩⊗|φ2i⟩⊗|i⟩|\Omega\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{k}}\sum_{i=1}^{k}|\varphi^{i}_{1}\rangle\otimes|\varphi^{i}_{2}\rangle\otimes|i\rangle is a unit vector in ℋ1⊗ℋ2⊗𝒦\mathcal{H}_{1}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{2}\otimes\mathcal{K}.

In what follows (speaking about the Schmidt rank and the Schmidt number) we will treat the space ℋ1⊗ℋ2⊗𝒦\mathcal{H}_{1}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{2}\otimes\mathcal{K} as the tensor product of the spaces ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} and ℋ2⊗𝒦\mathcal{H}_{2}\otimes\mathcal{K}.

Suppose that
